**UPDATE Wednesday 08-04-2026**

Orion emerged from behind the Moon and resumed communication with mission control after the blackout. [The Planetary Society](https://www.planetary.org/articles/artemis-ii-what-to-expect) The spacecraft reached its closest approach at about 7 p.m. ET, coming within 4,067 miles of the lunar surface, and set a new human spaceflight distance record of 252,756 miles from Earth. [NPR](https://www.npr.org/2026/04/06/nx-s1-5773187/nasa-artemis-ii-moon-lunar-flyby)

And the crew experienced more than just the flyby: At 8:35 p.m. they witnessed a solar eclipse as the Sun slipped behind the Moon for nearly an hour from Orion's perspective [NPR](https://www.npr.org/2026/04/06/nx-s1-5773187/nasa-artemis-ii-moon-lunar-flyby), giving them a chance to observe the corona and potentially lunar dust illuminated by sunlight. Commander Wiseman described seeing Mars and the "planet train" line up after the eclipse. [CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2026/04/06/science/live-news/nasa-artemis-2-flyby-moon-mission)

Jeremy Hansen's words from the far side are worth sitting with: "When we were on the far side of the moon, looking back at Earth, you really felt like you weren't in a capsule. You'd been transported to the far side of the moon. And it really just bent your mind." [CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2026/04/06/science/live-news/nasa-artemis-2-flyby-moon-mission) That's the Triple Vortex medicine doing its work — the void encountered, the mind bent, the return carrying something new.

Christina Koch on the Pathfinder-down moment turning into something else entirely: "One of the biggest highlights was coming back from the far side of the moon and having the first glimpses of planet Earth again after being out of communication for about 45 minutes." [CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2026/04/06/science/live-news/nasa-artemis-2-flyby-moon-mission)   
The lost path became the most profound perspective shift of the mission.

Here’s Victor Glover’s message back to Earth:   
“And as we are so far from earth and looking back at you know the beauty of creation, I think the for me one of the really important personal perspectives that I have up here is I can really see earth as one thing. And you know when I read the Bible and I look at all of the amazing things that were done for us who were created, it's you you have this amazing place, this spaceship. You guys are talking to us because we're in a spaceship really far from Earth. But you're on a spaceship called Earth that was created to give us a place to live in the universe in the cosmos. Think maybe the distance we are from you makes you think what we're doing is special, but we're the same distance from you. And I'm trying to tell you, just trust me, you are special. Whether you believe in God or not, um, this is an opportunity for us to remember where we are, who we are, and that we are the same thing, and that we got to get through this together.” 

The crew is now heading home. Days 7-9 involve trajectory corrections, rest, a radiation shelter construction demo, and manual piloting tests. Splashdown is targeted for April 10 off San Diego. [The Planetary Society](https://www.planetary.org/articles/artemis-ii-what-to-expect)

They encountered the void, navigated confinement, tapped the deep well, and emerged speaking universal love.

**UPDATE Saturday 11-04-2026 \- After Splashdown**

The Artemis 2 crew is home. Orion splashed down in the Pacific off the San Diego coast on April 10, and the four astronauts (Wiseman, Glover, Koch, and Hansen) were safely recovered. Ground control and independent mission watchers noted the trajectory was near-perfect on return, fitting for a mission that cancelled its first correction burn because they were already exactly where they needed to be.

And then there was the Nutella jar:   
The 6-Abundance(up) card had its quiet cameo when crew photos surfaced of an actual Nutella jar floating along inside Orion ([Universe Magazine](https://universemagazine.com/en/a-jar-of-nutella-accidentally-became-a-record-breaker-in-space/)). Astronaut food, apparently, and a reminder that even on humanity's first deep-space crewed mission in over fifty years, someone packed the good stuff. The optimal forager's calculus checks out: High nutritional density, low handling time, morale multiplier substantial. Abundance(up) doesn't always look like grand resources. Sometimes it looks like a hazelnut spread surviving lunar transit.

**Final pattern check:**

The reading from April 3rd mapped the mission's territory with uncomfortable precision. The Hook-down shadow showed up as the recurring toilet saga that became the mission's running joke and its most stubborn technical thread. The Abundance-up present held: Precise trajectory, working systems where it mattered, exceptional crew performance, and yes, the Nutella. The Pathfinder-down future arrived exactly on schedule as the 45-minute radio blackout behind the Moon, and transformed, in Christina Koch's own words, into the mission's most profound moment of perspective.

The 困/井 hexagram pair completed its arc: confinement met its well, the source held, and the crew returned carrying what the void gave them. Triple Vortex did its full alchemical sequence: Chaos encountered, distortion resisted, medicine radiated outward as Glover's message about being on a shared spaceship called Earth.

The reading didn't predict outcomes. It mapped territory. The territory was navigated. The well never runs dry.

***Welcome home, Artemis 2\. 🌙***
